title: Search inside a support inbox
excerpt: Search should find a conversation by the customer's words, name, or order number, and return to that thread without throwing away a draft. Say when a filter caused the empty list.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back, two ways of looking at the same object.
caption: The face and the back are both part of finding the thing. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should support search match?
faqs.answer: Customer name, email, order number, public messages, and saved-reply titles. Internal notes only for roles who may read notes. Rank open conversations above ancient resolved ones unless the query is clearly historical. Group snippets and conversations so a refund macro does not bury the live thread.

faqs.question: How do you keep search from eating a draft?
faqs.answer: Open results in a panel, or ask before leaving a composer that has text. Losing the draft is a worse failure than a weak match. From an old thread, leave a way back to the queue and to the results with the query still filled in.

faqs.question: Why does search sometimes show nothing for a real customer?
faqs.answer: A sticky filter is the usual cause. Show the chips, and say they are why the list is empty, with one tap to clear them. Also separate a true empty from a search that did not run. Those are different sentences.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Agents open support inbox search ux when the queue, the filters, and the assignment list have not surfaced the conversation they need. Show matches in the customer's language, and show a way back to the thread, or back to the next conversation if this was a detour.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay found that readers get through only about a quarter of the text on a page, and that they often leave in 10 to 20 seconds when the point is unclear. A search result that is a paragraph of ticket history will be skipped. The customer's words, the name, and the date will not.

## What they type on a shift

Agents type a name, an email, an order number, a phrase the customer used, or a promise someone made. "Mina." "Order 4412." "Replacement." "The warehouse." They are usually under a clock. They are not exploring your taxonomy. They already looked at My queue and did not see the thread, or a customer is on the phone quoting a sentence from last month.

Leads type a teammate's name, a tag, or "waiting since Monday." Admins type a mailbox or a channel. If one box serves all of this, the placeholder has to be honest, or the groups of results have to be obvious. "Search conversations, customers, and saved replies" is a contract. "Search" is not.

Do not make search the only way to see today's queue. The first screen is the next conversation. Search is the repair when someone cites an old promise, a missing order, or a thread that was assigned to a person who is out. If agents must search to find what they should answer next, the queue is wrong. Fix the queue.

## Matches in their words

Return the conversation, with the customer's line that matched, not your internal subject if the internal subject is a code. "Where is order 4412" beats "Ticket T-4412, status pending, priority normal." Put the matched phrase in the title or the first snippet. Agents will not read metadata to discover whether the hit is real.

Include the date, the channel, and who it is assigned to, on the same row, after the words. "Mina · email · yesterday · with Sam." That row can be scanned. A card with a portrait and three paragraphs cannot. Rank open and recently waiting conversations above ancient resolved ones, unless the query is clearly historical, such as a full email address or an old order number. When they are on the phone, the live thread outranks the archive. Say so by sort order, not by a help tooltip.

Saved replies are a different kind of result. If they typed "refund," they may want the snippet, or the conversations about refunds. Group them. Snippets first only when the composer is focused. Conversations first when they are in the queue. Context should change the ranking. A single global score will be wrong half the day.

Recent searches and recent conversations, shown when the box is empty, help the agent who jumped to search and forgot the name by the time the box focused. Recents are not a history product. Four or five items are enough.

## A way back to the work

Opening a result should not eat the reply they were writing. If a composer has a draft, search should open in a way that keeps it, or you should ask before navigating away. Losing a draft is a worse failure than a weak search. Many "search is broken" complaints are really "search threw away my work."

Once they are in the old thread, give them a return to the queue and a return to the results, with the query preserved. The phone call may require two threads. They will bounce. A back button that reloads an empty inbox is a trap.

If the match is a conversation they cannot open, say why on the row. "Assigned to the billing team. You can see the subject and not the thread." Or omit it entirely if the subject itself is sensitive. Pick the policy and make the empty-or-locked state use it. A result that 403s after the click feels like a bug, which is the feeling this whole pattern is supposed to avoid.

Related records, the order, the tracking page, can be results when the query is an order number. Land them on the conversation if one exists, and show the order in the margin. Land them on the order only if no conversation exists, with a way to start one. Do not invent a third destination that is a raw database row.

## Filters, tags, and false empties

Tags and status filters are part of the query. Show them as chips. "refund · open · last 30 days." If the result is empty, the sentence should name the chips. "No open conversations tagged refund in the last 30 days. Clear the date, or include resolved." One tap to clear. A filter that persists from yesterday and hides today's Mina is a classic shift-start bug. When they focus search, either clear sticky filters or announce them so loudly that they cannot miss the cause.

Empty and zero are different from failure. "No conversations match 'northwind.'" is an empty. "Search did not run. Try again." is a failure. "Filtered to Sam, and you typed Mina." is a conflict between filter and query. Write all three. An illustration of a magnifying glass does not distinguish them.

Spelling and email fragments should get a close match, labeled. "No customer named Mina K. Mina Khan has an open email from this morning." Do not silently open Mina Khan. The agent may be about to tell the wrong person their order status. Confirmation is the kind thing.

## What you index, and what you refuse

Index customer name, email, order numbers, the public messages, and the titles of saved replies. Index internal notes for people who are allowed to read notes, and exclude them for everyone else. A contractor who can search their way into a note about a different customer is a permissions bug with a search box on top.

Do not index other customers' payment data into a general box. An order number the agent is allowed to see can match. A card fingerprint must not. Say, under the box, what this role's search covers. "Your conversations, and customers assigned to your team. Not other teams' notes." The sentence will feel restrictive the first week and will prevent a leak the first month.

Order numbers deserve an exact mode. If the query is mostly digits, prefer the order that matches those digits over a conversation that happens to contain them in a timestamp or a phone number. Show the order id on the row so the agent can confirm before they open it. A near miss on an order id is worse than a miss, because the agent may tell the person on the phone the status of someone else's parcel. Exact, then close, and label the close ones.

Speed matters because the customer is often present, on the phone or in the chat, while the agent searches. Keep the current thread on screen. Results can arrive in a panel. A full-page search that takes the thread away will make agents split their attention across browser tabs, and then collision errors return. The panel can move with a small transition. The transition is not the feature.

## Review it on real phrases

Run the five phrases while a draft is open, and again with the queue filtered. The draft has to survive. The filter has to announce itself. Then run them as the contractor role, not as the owner, because the owner's search will look fine and the contractor's is the one that leaks or blocks. If the contractor cannot find the order you assigned them, the index is wrong. If they can find an order you did not assign, the scope is wrong. Fix scope before you touch synonyms.

Take five phrases from last week's real mail. A first name. An order number. A snippet title. A sentence from an internal note, searched by someone who may read notes and by someone who may not. A query that should be empty. If the note leaks, stop. If the order number lands on a raw record with no path back to the thread, fix the destination. If the first name returns fifty people, show the email and the last message on each row so the right Mina can be chosen without opening all fifty.

Say the order id in the agent's voice when you read the row back, including the channel. "Email from Mina, order 4412, open, with Sam." If that sentence is hard to form from the row, the row is missing a field. Add the field. Do not add a second paragraph under it. The phone call does not have room for a paragraph, and Nielsen Norman Group's point about how little of a page gets read applies twice as hard when a customer is waiting on the line.

The other place agents go when the inbox misbehaves is the cabinet: signatures, hours, assignment rules, the mailbox connection. [Settings in a support inbox](/blog/settings-in-a-support-inbox) is the next piece. Those controls should stay a cabinet, so search is not how someone changes the queue's rules.

If your team keeps a side spreadsheet of "who promised what" because search cannot find the promise, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring five real queries from last week. The right result for each one is a product decision, not a ranking tweak.
